messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Vulnerability: Being naked, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The trauma that still governs Thien’s life happened twenty-two years ago, during a deployment in a dense, humid region he has never named aloud to anyone except his wife, and even then only in fragments. He was a radio operator, and his unit was ambushed while moving through a narrow valley at dusk. What he remembers most vividly is not the gunfire itself but the smell—the thick, sweet rot of wet earth mixed with diesel fuel and something metallic, the smell of the river that ran alongside the road and the smoke from a burning supply truck. That smell comes back to him without warning. It arrives in his kitchen when his wife fries shallots in oil, or in the parking lot of his office building after a rain shower, and when it does, he hears the sounds again: the flat crack of small-arms fire, the urgent shouting, the high-pitched whine of a motorcycle engine that belonged to one of the scouts who was hit. That particular sound—a two-stroke engine revving—has become a kind of auditory trap. A motorcycle passing his house on the main road will stop him mid-sentence. He will freeze, and for a few seconds he is not in his living room but back in that valley, watching the scout fall.

Thien cannot put the event into words. When his therapist asks him to describe what happened, he shakes his head. The memory is not a story he can tell; it is a film that plays over and over, always the same scenes, always without language. He sees the mud on his hands, the way the light shifted through the canopy, the scout’s helmet rolling sideways. But he cannot narrate it. The images and sounds and smells arrive whole, and they arrive without his permission.

For years, Thien managed. He worked, he married, he raised two children. But after a company-wide restructuring two years ago, his avoidance tightened like a vise. He stopped watching television altogether—not just news or war films, but any programme that might contain a sudden loud noise or a scene of violence. He stopped reading novels. He stopped going out. He used to run three times a week, a loop through the park near his home, but one morning a motorcycle backfired on the street beside him and he spent the next hour on a bench, shaking, unable to stand. He has not exercised since. Running, which once cleared his mind, now feels like exposure.

At home, Thien is never fully off guard. He sits with his back to the wall. He checks the locks three times before bed. He has come to believe that strangers are a danger he cannot assess, so he avoids unfamiliar places entirely. He drives the same route to work every day. He eats lunch at his desk. When a new hire in his team—a young man with a loud voice and an unpredictable laugh—walked up to his cubicle to introduce himself, Thien felt his chest tighten and his vision narrow. He knew, intellectually, that the man was harmless. But his body did not believe it. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood in a stall for ten minutes, breathing slowly, waiting for the feeling to pass.

The most difficult trigger, and the one he finds most shameful, is being naked. He cannot explain why. There is no logical connection between the ambush and his own bare skin. But undressing for a shower, or standing in the bedroom with his clothes off, makes him feel exposed in a way that is intolerable. He has begun to shower with the bathroom door locked and the light off, as if darkness might protect him. His wife has noticed. She has asked him, gently, what is wrong. He has not told her.

What finally brought Thien to seek help was a panic attack in the grocery store. A shopper walked past him carrying a bag of charcoal, and the smell—smoke and lighter fluid and something organic—sent him reeling. He dropped his basket. He left the cart in the aisle and walked out into the parking lot, and he stood there, in the rain, unable to go back inside. He drove home and sat in the car in the driveway for forty minutes before he could open the door.

Now he is sitting in a clinician’s office, a man who has built his life around control and predictability, and he is afraid. He is afraid that talking about the ambush will make the film play louder. He is afraid that he will never be able to run again, or watch a movie with his wife, or walk into a store without smelling smoke. But he is also, beneath the fear, hoping for something he cannot quite name—a kind of quiet, perhaps, or a door that he can open without bracing himself for what is on the other side.
